newsitem.title: USA: Pennzoil has no choice but to talk to UPR. [CORRECTED 00:29 GMT 23/7]
newsitem.headline: Pennzoil has no choice but to talk to UPR. [CORRECTED 00:29 GMT 23/7]

text.p: A resoundingly successful outcome for Union Pacific Resources Group Inc's tender in the first round of its hostile bid for Pennzoil Co has left that company's board no choice but to talk to the aggressor, say analysts.
On Tuesday, UPR said that 61.5 percent (corrects from 65.1 percent) of Pennzoil's shareholders had backed the first part of its $84 per share cash and stock offer for Pennzoil.
But Pennzoil responded saying that it still believed UPR's offer was divisive and that its present board could deliver better value, a stance that analysts say is unsustainable.
"These are very strong tender offer results, it is overwhelming for Pennzoil's board," said Michael Young, analyst at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.
Pennzoil shares fell 0-1/8 to 76-1/2 and Union Pacific was up 0-1/16 at 23-3/4 after the announcement.

Pennzoil's board says that the cash and stock offer was designed to coerce its shareholders as those that did not tender for cash would be left holding UPR stock in the second part of the deal, under which UPR wants to pay for 49.9 percent of Pennzoil using its own stock.

"Because of UPR's market performance and the pricing collar mechanism that limits the value of the second step transaction, the purported value of any UPR stock to be delivered is subject to substantial pressure and uncertainty, particularly when UPR trades below $25 a share," said James Pate, Pennzoil's chief executive.
UPR's stock has fallen from 26-3/8 since it launched its offer and this devalues its bid.
However, the company has repeatedly offered to talk to the Pennzoil board and analysts say this could lead to an all-cash offer or an improvement in the price.

"From the tone of the Pennzoil statement, they are just carping about the structure of the deal. The rest of it is a so what statement about their earnings and no one seriously believes they can generate better value than UPR's bid at least in the short term," said one analyst who declined to be named.
Despite the high level of acceptances, Union Pacific still has to talk to Pennzoil's board if it wants to win the company.
The company can tie up the bid in the courts for years and has a whole range of anti-takeover measures and a poison-pill defence.
"Pennzoil is very concerned about the structure of the deal, the best way to eliminate that is to negotiate terms," said Young. ((-- David Chance New York Newsroom 212 859 1902))
